distributed-systems-fundamentals::CAP th.title: CAP theorem
distributed-systems-fundamentals::CAP th.summary: During a network partition, a replicated system must choose per operation between one consistent history and a successful response from every side.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::CAP th.tradeoff: Partition tolerance makes the consistency-versus-availability choice unavoidable.

mechanism.scenario: A checkout preference is replicated across two regions when the inter-region link partitions.

entities.label: West replica
entities.description: Accepts traffic in the west region

entities.label: East replica
entities.description: Accepts traffic in the east region

frames.title: Replicas agree
frames.narration: Both regions expose version 7 before the partition.
frames.outcome: The system starts consistent and available.
frames.invariant: CAP constrains behavior only when communication needed for an operation is partitioned.

frames.title: Link partitions
frames.narration: The inter-region path drops replication and acknowledgements.
frames.outcome: Each side can still receive local requests but cannot coordinate.
frames.invariant: A partition prevents simultaneously guaranteeing one history and success from both sides.

frames.title: CP choice rejects
frames.narration: West requires cross-region agreement and refuses the write.
frames.outcome: Consistency is preserved by sacrificing write availability.
frames.invariant: No acknowledged write may exist on only one side under the CP policy.

frames.title: AP choice accepts
frames.narration: With the policy switched to availability, west accepts a local version 8.
frames.outcome: Both sides remain available but expose divergent values.
frames.invariant: An AP response cannot promise linearizable cross-partition reads.

frames.title: Partition heals
frames.narration: Replication resumes and the conflict rule selects west version 8.
frames.outcome: The replicas converge after connectivity returns.
frames.invariant: CAP does not prescribe the reconciliation rule; the application must define it.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::PACELC.title: PACELC
distributed-systems-fundamentals::PACELC.summary: PACELC extends CAP: during partitions choose availability or consistency; otherwise choose latency or consistency.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::PACELC.tradeoff: Replica coordination costs latency even without failures.

mechanism.scenario: PACELC extends CAP: during partitions choose availability or consistency; otherwise choose latency or consistency.

frames.title: Step 1

frames.title: Step 2
frames.narration: Under partition, choose availability or coordinated consistency.

frames.title: Step 3
frames.narration: Without partition, choose lower latency or stronger replica agreement.

frames.title: Step 4
frames.narration: Apply the selected policy per operation and document both choices.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Consis.title: Consistency models
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Consis.summary: A consistency model defines which values operations may observe under concurrency and failure.

mechanism.scenario: A consistency model defines which values operations may observe under concurrency and failure.

frames.title: Step 1

frames.title: Step 2

frames.title: Step 3
frames.narration: A reader may observe v1, v2, or an ordered sequence.

frames.title: Step 4

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Strong.title: Strong consistency
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Strong.summary: Strong consistency presents completed updates through one authoritative view, commonly with real-time ordering.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Strong.tradeoff: Coordination raises latency and can reduce partition availability.

mechanism.scenario: Strong consistency presents completed updates through one authoritative view, commonly with real-time ordering.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Linear.title: Linearizability
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Linear.summary: Each operation appears atomic between invocation and response while respecting real-time order.

mechanism.scenario: Two clients update and read one inventory register while a primary orders operations.

frames.title: Initial register
frames.narration: The primary stores stock 5 at version 21.
frames.outcome: All participants begin from version 21.
frames.invariant: A linearizable register has one legal sequential history.

frames.title: Write begins
frames.narration: Writer A invokes a conditional decrement.
frames.outcome: The operation is in flight and has not yet taken effect.
frames.invariant: The linearization point must lie between invocation and response.

frames.title: Write linearizes
frames.narration: The primary atomically installs version 22.
frames.outcome: Stock 4 becomes the only current value.
frames.invariant: No reader may observe a partial atomic update.

frames.title: Response precedes read
frames.narration: The write completes before Reader B starts.
frames.outcome: Real-time order constrains the later read.
frames.invariant: If A completes before B begins, B must be ordered after A.

frames.title: Read sees latest
frames.narration: Reader B receives stock 4 from version 22.
frames.outcome: The observed result matches the real-time sequential history.
frames.invariant: A completed write cannot be hidden from a later linearizable read.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Sequen.title: Sequential consistency
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Sequen.summary: All operations appear in one order that preserves each participant program order, but not necessarily wall-clock order.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Sequen.tradeoff: Weaker than linearizability and still requires global ordering.

mechanism.scenario: All operations appear in one order that preserves each participant program order, but not necessarily wall-clock order.

frames.title: Step 4

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Causal.title: Causal consistency
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Causal.summary: Causally related operations are observed in order while concurrent operations may be observed differently.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Causal.tradeoff: Needs causal metadata and session propagation.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Eventu.title: Eventual consistency
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Eventu.summary: Replicas may diverge temporarily but converge when updates stop and messages are delivered.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Eventu.tradeoff: Clients must tolerate stale reads and conflicts.

mechanism.scenario: A profile display name propagates asynchronously from a home replica to two remote replicas.

frames.title: Common baseline
frames.narration: Every replica stores display name Ana at version 42.

frames.title: First propagation

frames.invariant: A newer version must not be overwritten by an older delivery.

frames.title: Delayed replica catches up
frames.narration: APAC receives the queued mutation after a transient delay.
frames.outcome: All replicas expose the same value.
frames.invariant: If updates stop and messages arrive, replicas must converge.

frames.title: Anti-entropy verifies
frames.narration: A digest exchange confirms no replica is missing version 43.
frames.outcome: Convergence is detected rather than assumed.
frames.invariant: Eventual consistency alone provides no maximum staleness duration.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Quorum.title: Quorum reads/writes
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Quorum.summary: Reads contact R replicas and writes contact W of N; intersecting quorums can expose the latest accepted version.
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Quorum.tradeoff: Larger quorums increase latency and reduce availability.

frames.invariant: For strict quorum intersection, R + W must exceed N.

frames.title: Write fan-out
frames.narration: The coordinator sends version 12 to every replica.

frames.invariant: The coordinator must not report success before W replicas persist the version.

frames.title: Write quorum
frames.narration: R2 persists version 12, satisfying W=2.

frames.invariant: Any read quorum of two intersects the two-replica write quorum.

frames.title: Read quorum
frames.narration: A read contacts stale R3 and current R2.
frames.outcome: The coordinator selects version 12 by version order.
frames.invariant: Quorum intersection exposes at least one acknowledged latest version, assuming replicas preserve it.

frames.title: Read repair
frames.narration: The coordinator repairs stale R3 with version 12.
frames.outcome: All replicas converge without blocking the original write.
frames.invariant: Version comparison must reject repair with an older value.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Gossip.title: Gossip protocols
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Gossip.summary: Nodes repeatedly exchange partial membership or state until information converges probabilistically.

mechanism.scenario: Five membership agents disseminate that node E is unhealthy through randomized peer exchanges.

frames.title: Healthy view
frames.narration: Every live agent records E alive at incarnation 18.
frames.outcome: Membership views initially match.
frames.invariant: Incarnation numbers prevent older rumors from replacing newer membership state.

frames.title: Local suspicion
frames.narration: A misses E heartbeats and records a suspicion at incarnation 19.
frames.outcome: Only A knows the new status.
frames.invariant: Gossip begins with local evidence and does not require a central broadcaster.

frames.title: Random fan-out
frames.narration: A randomly selects C and transmits its delta.
frames.outcome: Two agents now carry the rumor.
frames.invariant: A merge keeps the greatest incarnation for each member.

frames.title: Epidemic spread
frames.narration: C tells D while D independently tells B.
frames.outcome: All reachable agents converge after several rounds.
frames.invariant: Convergence is probabilistic; redundant exchanges improve dissemination probability.

frames.title: Stable digest
frames.narration: Agents exchange equal digests and retain the newest rumor.
frames.outcome: No coordinator was needed to spread the failure view.
frames.invariant: A recovered E must refute suspicion with an incarnation greater than 19.

distributed-systems-fundamentals::Lampor.title: Lamport clocks
distributed-systems-fundamentals::Lampor.summary: Counters ensure that causal precedence implies increasing timestamps, with tie-breakers providing a total order.

frames.narration: B receives stamp 6 and advances to max(7,6)+1=8.
frames.outcome: The receive event is ordered after the send.

frames.outcome: The causal chain has increasing timestamps 6, 8, 9.
frames.invariant: Equal counters require a deterministic node-id tie-breaker for total sorting.

frames.outcome: The ledger can produce a total order consistent with causality.
frames.invariant: Lamport clocks cannot prove that two differently stamped events were concurrent.

frames.title: Merged descendant
frames.narration: The application merges both fields and emits vector [3,3].
frames.outcome: The merged document causally dominates both inputs.
frames.invariant: A merged vector takes component maxima and advances the merger’s writer component.

frames.title: A records a physical-time event
frames.narration: A reads millisecond 1000, which exceeds its prior physical component 995.
frames.outcome: A anchors the tuple to its advancing wall clock and resets the logical component.
frames.invariant: An HLC physical component never decreases.

frames.title: Clock regression increments logical time
frames.narration: A wall time regresses to 997, so a second local event retains physical 1000 and increments logical to one.
frames.outcome: The second event remains ordered after the first without moving backward in physical time.
frames.invariant: When wall time does not exceed stored physical time, a local event increments the logical component.

frames.title: A sends a stamped mutation
frames.narration: The send is an event, so A increments its logical component and attaches (1000,2).
frames.outcome: The message carries a timestamp later than both A updates.
frames.invariant: Every send advances the sender HLC before publishing its tuple.

frames.title: B merges a future remote tuple
frames.narration: B receives at physical 998 and chooses physical max 1000, then advances beyond the remote logical value to three.
frames.outcome: B is causally after A even though B wall time is behind.
frames.invariant: A receive timestamp must compare greater than the message timestamp.

frames.title: B wall clock catches up
frames.narration: At physical 1005, B records a local event and resets the logical component.
frames.outcome: Physical time resumes carrying the ordering once it exceeds the stored component.
frames.invariant: Logical time resets to zero only when the chosen physical component strictly advances.

frames.title: A merges B reply
frames.narration: B sends at (1005,1); A receives it at wall time 1002 and advances to (1005,2).
frames.outcome: The ledger has a causality-compatible order with timestamps close to wall time.
frames.invariant: HLC ties still require a deterministic node-id tie-breaker; HLC does not make physical clocks exact.

frames.title: Sender emits sequence 41
frames.narration: P assigns sequence 41 to debit before placing it on the channel.
frames.outcome: The packet carries enough metadata to recover P send order.
frames.invariant: One sender never reuses or decreases its sequence number within an epoch.

frames.title: Sender emits sequence 42
frames.narration: P sends receipt 42 after debit 41, but the channel gives it a shorter delay.
frames.outcome: Send order is 41 then 42 even though arrival order will differ.
frames.invariant: FIFO is scoped per sender; it does not compare unrelated senders.

frames.title: Early successor is held
frames.narration: Receipt 42 arrives first and cannot pass missing sequence 41.
frames.outcome: The application sees neither packet yet.
frames.invariant: A packet with sequence greater than nextExpected is buffered, never delivered early.

frames.title: Gap arrival drains contiguous order
frames.narration: Debit 41 arrives, is delivered, advances nextExpected to 42, and releases buffered receipt 42.
frames.outcome: Arrival order 42,41 becomes application order 41,42.
frames.invariant: Delivery advances only through a contiguous sequence prefix.

frames.title: Duplicate is discarded
frames.narration: A retransmitted receipt 42 arrives after nextExpected has advanced to 43.
frames.outcome: Retry traffic does not duplicate the application event.
frames.invariant: A sequence below nextExpected is stale or duplicate and cannot be redelivered under exactly-once FIFO delivery state.

frames.title: B wins the next slot
frames.narration: B proposal Y reaches the sequencer before queued X and receives slot 81.

frames.narration: No acceptor has promised or accepted a value for slot 12.

frames.invariant: A value is chosen only after acceptance by a quorum.

frames.title: Prepare quorum
frames.narration: P sends prepare 7 and receives promises from A1 and A2.
frames.outcome: A majority promises not to accept lower ballots.
frames.invariant: An acceptor persists its promise before replying.

frames.narration: No promise reports an earlier accepted value, so P may propose blue.
frames.outcome: The proposed value obeys the phase-one selection rule.
frames.invariant: If promises include accepted values, the proposer must use the value from the highest accepted ballot.

frames.title: Majority acceptance
frames.narration: A2 durably accepts ballot 7 value blue.
frames.outcome: Blue is chosen by the intersecting quorum A1,A2.
frames.invariant: Once chosen, every later successful ballot must preserve blue.

frames.title: Learner notified

frames.outcome: The decision survives one acceptor failure.
frames.invariant: Learner notification may lag without changing the chosen value.

probabilistic-data-structures::Quotient.title: Quotient filter
probabilistic-data-structures::Quotient.summary: Compact hash quotients and remainders support membership, deletion, and locality-friendly scans.
probabilistic-data-structures::Quotient.tradeoff: Performance degrades at high load factors.

mechanism.scenario: A cache admission index stores hash remainders in quotient-clustered slots while preserving enough metadata for lookup and deletion.

frames.title: Empty quotient table
frames.narration: Five slots begin with empty remainder fields and metadata bits occupied, continuation, and shifted all clear.
frames.outcome: No quotient has an occupied run.
frames.invariant: An empty slot has no remainder and no metadata bits.

frames.title: Insert first fingerprint
frames.narration: Hash 01|101 has quotient 1 and remainder 5, so remainder 5 occupies its home slot 1.
frames.outcome: Quotient 1 now owns a one-element run.
frames.invariant: The first remainder in a run has continuation=0.

frames.title: Extend the same run
frames.narration: Hash 01|010 shares quotient 1; remainder 2 sorts before 5 and shifts remainder 5 to slot 2.
frames.outcome: The q1 run is [2,5], with the displaced element marked shifted and continuation.
frames.invariant: Remainders inside one quotient run remain sorted.

frames.title: Create an adjacent run
frames.narration: Hash 10|011 has quotient 2; its home slot is occupied, so remainder 3 shifts to slot 3 and starts q2's run.
frames.outcome: One cluster now contains the q1 and q2 runs.
frames.invariant: Occupied marks a quotient home even when that quotient's first remainder is shifted elsewhere.

frames.title: Lookup by run scan
frames.narration: Lookup B splits to q1,r2, finds q1's run boundary, and matches remainder 2 before entering q2.
frames.outcome: The compact fingerprint is found without storing the original key.
frames.invariant: Lookup scans only the target quotient's sorted run; fingerprint collisions remain possible.

probabilistic-data-structures::HyperLogL.title: HyperLogLog

probabilistic-data-structures::HyperLogL.tradeoff: Returns a statistical estimate, not members.

mechanism.scenario: An analytics service estimates unique visitors without retaining IDs.

frames.title: Empty registers
frames.narration: Eight registers begin at zero.
frames.outcome: No cardinality is observed.
frames.invariant: Registers store maxima, never individual IDs.

frames.title: Observe u17
frames.narration: The hash prefix 010 selects R2; the suffix has rank 3.
frames.outcome: R2 records rank 3.
frames.invariant: A register is max(previous rank, observed rank).

frames.title: Observe more IDs
frames.narration: Independent hashes spread visitors and raise several maxima.
frames.outcome: Five distinct observations shape the register vector.
frames.invariant: Repeated IDs produce the same register/rank pair.

frames.title: Ignore a duplicate
frames.narration: u17 hashes exactly as before, leaving R2 at 3.
frames.outcome: The estimate is unchanged.
frames.invariant: Duplicate observations are idempotent.

frames.title: Harmonic estimate
frames.narration: The harmonic mean of 2^-register produces the corrected cardinality estimate.
frames.outcome: The sketch reports about seven unique visitors.
frames.invariant: Estimation depends only on the complete register vector.

probabilistic-data-structures::Count-Min.title: Count-Min Sketch
probabilistic-data-structures::Count-Min.summary: Hashed counter rows estimate frequency by taking the minimum counter for an item.

mechanism.scenario: A telemetry pipeline estimates request frequency for hot keys.

frames.title: Zero matrix
frames.narration: Three hash rows and five columns begin at zero.
frames.outcome: The sketch has no traffic.
frames.invariant: All counters are nonnegative.

frames.title: Count feed
frames.narration: GET /feed maps to columns 1, 3, and 0 and increments each.
frames.outcome: The estimated frequency is one.
frames.invariant: Each update touches one counter per row.

frames.title: Accumulate traffic
frames.narration: Four more feed requests raise the same three counters to five.
frames.outcome: The sketch reports five.
frames.invariant: Counters never decrease in the standard sketch.

frames.title: Collision adds noise
frames.narration: GET /home collides in row 0 column 1 but uses other columns in rows 1 and 2.
frames.outcome: Only one feed counter is polluted.
frames.invariant: Collisions can overcount but never undercount.

frames.title: Take row minimum
frames.narration: Querying feed reads 7, 5, and 5; the minimum limits collision error.
frames.outcome: The correct estimate remains five.
frames.invariant: The estimate is the minimum of the selected row counters.

mechanism.scenario: A telemetry stream uses four Space-Saving counters to retain likely high-frequency endpoint keys under bounded memory.

entities.label: A B A C A D E A

frames.title: Fill bounded counters
frames.narration: The first distinct keys A, B, C, and D occupy the four available slots.
frames.outcome: All observed keys are represented while capacity remains.
frames.invariant: Each slot stores key, estimated count, and insertion error.

frames.title: Increment tracked keys
frames.narration: Two more A events update A in place from one to three.
frames.outcome: A separates from the one-count tail.
frames.invariant: A tracked key increments without changing its error bound.

frames.title: Replace a minimum
frames.narration: Untracked E replaces minimum slot B; E receives estimate 2 and error 1.

action.label: replace B with E at count 2

frames.outcome: E is tracked without growing memory.
frames.invariant: A replacement estimate is old minimum plus one, and its error is the old minimum.

frames.title: Survive stream pressure
frames.narration: F, G, and another A replace low slots while A rises to four.

action.label: replace tail keys and increment A

frames.outcome: The dominant key remains stable while one-off keys churn.
frames.invariant: Any omitted key has true frequency no greater than the current minimum estimate.

frames.title: Report threshold candidates
frames.narration: For threshold 30% of ten events, only A's lower bound 4 exceeds three.
frames.outcome: A is emitted with estimate and lower bound four.
frames.invariant: A candidate is guaranteed heavy only when estimate minus error exceeds the threshold.

mechanism.scenario: A request monitor combines a Count-Min frequency sketch with a size-three candidate min-heap.

frames.title: Initialize sketch and heap
frames.narration: Two five-column rows are zero and the candidate heap is empty.
frames.outcome: The structure uses fixed sketch memory plus three candidate slots.
frames.invariant: Frequency estimates are row minima.

frames.title: Track early leaders
frames.narration: feed, search, and home update two counters each and fill the heap.
frames.outcome: Three one-count candidates are retained.
frames.invariant: The heap contains at most k distinct keys.

frames.title: Raise feed's estimate
frames.narration: Three additional feed events raise its selected counters and heap score to four.
frames.outcome: feed is protected from tail churn.
frames.invariant: Candidate scores are refreshed from the current sketch estimate.

frames.title: Apply tail pressure
frames.narration: Keys x, y, and z collide in some counters; x reaches estimate two and replaces one-count search.
frames.outcome: The heap adapts while CMS collisions may overestimate tail keys.
frames.invariant: A full heap admits only candidates whose estimate exceeds its minimum.

frames.title: Return approximate top K
frames.narration: A final home event raises it to two; sorting yields feed=4, home=2, x=2.
frames.outcome: The monitor returns a bounded approximate top three.
frames.invariant: Returned counts never understate true counts, but collisions can alter borderline membership.

probabilistic-data-structures::HyperLogL.title: HyperLogLog++
probabilistic-data-structures::HyperLogL.summary: HyperLogLog++ improves small-cardinality bias, sparse representation, and estimator accuracy.
probabilistic-data-structures::HyperLogL.tradeoff: More implementation complexity than basic HyperLogLog.

mechanism.scenario: A cardinality sketch starts with sparse encoded registers, converts to dense storage, and applies small-range and bias corrections.

frames.title: Begin in sparse mode
frames.narration: Only nonzero register/rank pairs are encoded while cardinality is tiny.
frames.outcome: Two occupied registers consume less space than a dense array.
frames.invariant: A register stores the maximum observed rank for its index.

frames.title: Ignore duplicate evidence
frames.narration: A repeated element hashes to r2 with rank 3 and leaves the sparse map unchanged.
frames.outcome: Duplicate input does not increase the estimate.
frames.invariant: Register updates are idempotent maxima.

frames.title: Cross the sparse threshold
frames.narration: New occupied registers make sparse encoding larger than eight dense registers, triggering conversion.
frames.outcome: All maxima survive in a fixed dense vector.
frames.invariant: Mode conversion changes representation, not register values.

frames.title: Apply small-range correction
frames.narration: With one zero register and a small raw estimate, linear counting m·ln(m/V) gives 16.6 rather than raw 7.8.
frames.outcome: The estimator selects the calibrated small-cardinality regime.
frames.invariant: Correction choice depends on range and zero-register count, not event order.

frames.title: Use bias-corrected dense estimate
frames.narration: After more observations remove all zeros, raw 31.4 minus empirical bias 1.8 yields 29.6.
frames.outcome: The sketch reports about thirty unique values.
frames.invariant: Dense estimation uses the full register vector and a bias table calibrated for its precision.

mechanism.scenario: A linear-counting bitmap estimates unique device IDs from the fraction of zero bits and exposes collision error.

frames.title: Start with sixteen zeros
frames.narration: The bitmap has m=16 available positions and estimate zero.
frames.outcome: No distinct devices are represented.
frames.invariant: Bits only transition from zero to one.

frames.title: Set three distinct positions
frames.narration: u1, u2, and u3 hash to positions 2, 7, and 11.
frames.outcome: The estimate is close to the exact distinct count three.
frames.invariant: Estimator state depends on occupied positions, not total events.

frames.title: Ignore a duplicate
frames.narration: A repeated u1 selects already-set bit 2 and changes neither zeros nor estimate.
frames.outcome: Duplicate traffic is idempotent.
frames.invariant: Setting a one bit again cannot increase distinct evidence.

frames.title: Expose a hash collision
frames.narration: New device u4 also hashes to bit 7, so exact distinct count rises while the bitmap does not.
frames.outcome: Collision causes underestimation in this sample.
frames.invariant: The bitmap cannot distinguish IDs sharing a position.

frames.title: Estimate after more occupancy
frames.narration: Four more unique IDs set bits 0, 5, 9, and 14; V=9 yields estimate 9.21 for exact eight.
frames.outcome: The displayed error quantifies this sketch realization.
frames.invariant: Linear counting is valid while enough zero bits remain; saturation requires a larger bitmap.

probabilistic-data-structures::Probabili.title: Probabilistic counters
probabilistic-data-structures::Probabili.summary: Counters update with decreasing probability as values grow, representing large counts in few bits.

mechanism.scenario: A Morris counter represents a large event count with one small exponent and randomized increment probability.

frames.title: Initialize exponent zero
frames.narration: Register c=0 decodes to estimate zero before any event.
frames.outcome: One tiny register represents the count state.
frames.invariant: Decoded estimate is 2^c minus one.

frames.title: First event always increments
frames.narration: At c=0 the increment probability is one, so e1 raises c to one.
frames.outcome: The estimate exactly matches one.
frames.invariant: The gate probability before increment is 2^-c.

frames.title: Randomly skip at c=1
frames.narration: For e2, U=0.72 exceeds probability one-half, so c stays one.
frames.outcome: The compact estimate temporarily trails the exact count.
frames.invariant: A skipped event changes exact truth but not the register.

frames.title: Advance to exponent three
frames.narration: Accepted draws at later events raise c from one to two and then three.
frames.outcome: At seven events the decoded estimate is seven.
frames.invariant: Increment probability halves each time the exponent rises.

frames.title: Show error at twelve events
frames.narration: Five more events produce no accepted 1/8 draw, leaving estimate seven for exact twelve.
frames.outcome: The single run has relative error -41.7%; averaging counters can reduce variance.
frames.invariant: The estimator is unbiased over randomness even though individual trajectories vary.

probabilistic-data-structures::MinHash.title: MinHash
probabilistic-data-structures::MinHash.summary: Minimum hash signatures estimate Jaccard similarity between sets.
probabilistic-data-structures::MinHash.tradeoff: More signature components improve accuracy at memory cost.

mechanism.scenario: A near-duplicate detector compares two document shingle sets using four shared hash permutations and their row minima.

frames.title: Expose the two sets
frames.narration: A and B share ab, bc, and de; their union also contains cd and xy.
frames.outcome: Actual Jaccard similarity is 3/5 or 0.60.
frames.invariant: MinHash uses identical hash functions for both sets.

frames.title: Retain h1 minima
frames.narration: Under h1, ab is minimum for both sets, producing matching first signature entries.
frames.outcome: Row h1 contributes one signature match.
frames.invariant: A row stores only the minimum hash value per set.

frames.title: Add h2 and h3 minima
frames.narration: h2 minima differ because cd wins A while xy wins B; h3 minima match on bc.

action.label: retain h2 mismatch and h3 match

frames.outcome: Two of three signature rows match.
frames.invariant: Each row minimum is independent evidence that a shared shingle wins the permutation.

frames.title: Complete four-row signatures
frames.narration: h4 chooses de for both sets, yielding A=[2,1,4,0] and B=[2,3,4,0].
frames.outcome: Three of four minima match.
frames.invariant: Signature coordinates compare only corresponding hash rows.

frames.title: Compare estimate with intuition
frames.narration: The matching-signature fraction is 3/4=0.75 versus actual Jaccard 3/5=0.60.
frames.outcome: Four rows give a noisy but compact similarity estimate.
frames.invariant: Expected signature agreement equals Jaccard; more independent rows reduce variance.

probabilistic-data-structures::SimHash.title: SimHash
probabilistic-data-structures::SimHash.summary: A weighted bit signature preserves angular similarity and supports near-duplicate detection by Hamming distance.
probabilistic-data-structures::SimHash.tradeoff: Best for cosine-like similarity, not arbitrary distance metrics.

mechanism.scenario: A document deduplicator projects weighted features into signed bit accumulators and compares fingerprints by Hamming distance.

frames.title: Assign weighted features
frames.narration: Document A contributes cat weight 3, sat weight 2, and mat weight 1.
frames.outcome: Feature importance is explicit before bit projection.
frames.invariant: The same feature always has the same hash bits.

frames.title: Accumulate cat signs
frames.narration: cat=1010 adds +3,-3,+3,-3 to the four signed accumulators.
frames.outcome: Each hash bit votes with the feature's weight.
frames.invariant: Bit one adds weight and bit zero subtracts weight.

frames.title: Add remaining features
frames.narration: sat and mat update the final accumulator vector to [+4,-4,+2,0].

action.label: add sat and mat signed weights

frames.outcome: All weighted feature evidence is compressed into four sums.
frames.invariant: Feature order does not affect accumulator totals.

frames.title: Threshold the fingerprint
frames.narration: Positive accumulators become one; nonpositive values become zero, producing A=1010.
frames.outcome: Document A has a four-bit SimHash.
frames.invariant: Each fingerprint bit records only the accumulator sign.

frames.title: Measure near-duplicate distance
frames.narration: A=1010 XOR B=1110 gives 0100 with popcount one.

action.label: xor A with B and popcount

frames.outcome: At threshold one, B is a near-duplicate candidate.
frames.invariant: Hamming distance counts differing fingerprint positions, not differing raw features.

probabilistic-data-structures::Reservoir.title: Reservoir sampling
probabilistic-data-structures::Reservoir.summary: A fixed-size uniform sample is maintained from a stream of unknown length.

mechanism.scenario: A log service keeps a uniform sample of three events from an unbounded stream.

entities.label: e1 e2 e3 e4 e5 e6

frames.title: Fill slot zero
frames.narration: The first event occupies the first of k=3 slots.
frames.outcome: e1 is retained.
frames.invariant: The first k events are admitted directly.

frames.title: Fill reservoir
frames.narration: Events e2 and e3 complete the initial sample.
frames.outcome: All three slots are occupied.
frames.invariant: After k arrivals, every seen item is represented.

frames.title: Replace for e4
frames.narration: For item 4, draw j=1 from [0,3]; because j<3, slot 1 is replaced.
frames.outcome: e4 replaces e2.
frames.invariant: Each of four seen items has retention probability 3/4.

frames.title: Skip e5
frames.narration: For item 5, draw j=4; j is outside the reservoir, so no slot changes.
frames.outcome: The sample stays unchanged.
frames.invariant: Acceptance probability at item i is k/i.

frames.title: Replace for e6
frames.narration: For item 6, draw j=0 and replace slot zero.
frames.outcome: The final sample is e6, e4, e3.
frames.invariant: Every one of six events has equal probability 3/6 of retention.

probabilistic-data-structures::Sampling.title: Sampling algorithms
probabilistic-data-structures::Sampling.summary: Uniform, weighted, stratified, or adaptive sampling reduces data while preserving defined statistical properties.
probabilistic-data-structures::Sampling.tradeoff: Incorrect sampling frames create biased conclusions.

mechanism.scenario: A uniform reservoir sampler of size three contrasts deterministic initial fill with randomized replacement and rejection decisions.

entities.label: e1 e2 e3 e4 e5 e6

frames.title: Admit the first item
frames.narration: With capacity k=3, e1 deterministically occupies slot zero.
frames.outcome: The sample contains every item seen so far.
frames.invariant: The first k stream items are selected with probability one.

frames.title: Complete deterministic fill
frames.narration: e2 and e3 occupy the remaining slots without random draws.
frames.outcome: The reservoir is full with three uniformly retained items.
frames.invariant: Before item k+1, no item has been excluded.

frames.title: Replace uniformly for e4
frames.narration: For i=4, draw j=1 from [0,4); because j<3, e4 replaces slot one.
frames.outcome: Each of four items now has retention probability 3/4.
frames.invariant: A selected replacement slot is uniform among k slots.

frames.title: Reject e5
frames.narration: For i=5, draw j=4; because j is not a reservoir index, e5 is discarded.
frames.outcome: Random rejection leaves all slots unchanged.
frames.invariant: Item i is accepted with probability k/i.

frames.title: Replace again for e6
frames.narration: For i=6, draw j=0 and replace e1, yielding [e6,e4,e3].
frames.outcome: Every one of six events has equal final inclusion probability one-half.
frames.invariant: Uniformity follows from admission k/i and uniform eviction among current slots.

distributed-messaging-eventing::Event so.title: Event sourcing
distributed-messaging-eventing::Event so.summary: Immutable domain events are authoritative and current state is reconstructed by replay or snapshots.
distributed-messaging-eventing::Event so.tradeoff: Event evolution and projection repair are complex.

mechanism.scenario: A community bank reconstructs account A-12 from immutable deposits, withdrawals, and a snapshot.

frames.title: Load snapshot and tail
frames.narration: The handler loads snapshot v20 at $800, then replays a $100 deposit and $60 withdrawal.
frames.outcome: Current aggregate state is derived, not read from a mutable authoritative row.
frames.invariant: Replaying the same ordered facts produces the same account state.

frames.title: Validate the command
frames.narration: Withdrawal W-9 requests $200; the reconstructed $840 balance satisfies the no-overdraft rule.
frames.outcome: Business validation uses reconstructed aggregate state.
frames.invariant: Commands express intent; only accepted outcomes become immutable events.

frames.title: Append with expected version
frames.narration: MoneyWithdrawn $200 appends as v23 only if the stream is still at expected version 22.
frames.outcome: Optimistic concurrency prevents two writers from silently forking A-12.
frames.invariant: Events append; previously committed account facts are never updated in place.

frames.title: Update the projection asynchronously
frames.narration: The projector consumes v23 and writes the query-optimized balance.
frames.outcome: The read model catches up from $840 to $640 and can be rebuilt if corrupted.
frames.invariant: Projection handlers are idempotent and checkpoint only after applying an event.

frames.title: Rebuild from history
frames.narration: A repair clears the projection and replays through v23, reproducing $640.
frames.outcome: Immutable history repairs the derived view and supports new projections.
frames.invariant: Snapshots optimize replay but never replace the authoritative event stream.

distributed-transactions::Two-phase comm.title: Two-phase commit (2PC)
distributed-transactions::Two-phase comm.summary: Participants durably prepare before a coordinator records and broadcasts commit or abort.
distributed-transactions::Two-phase comm.tradeoff: Prepared resources can block during coordinator failure.

mechanism.scenario: A travel desk atomically books the last seat and a hotel room for trip TX-42.

entities.label: Trip coordinator
entities.description: records the durable global decision for TX-42

frames.title: Begin one global booking
frames.narration: The coordinator assigns TX-42 before either supplier changes visible availability.
frames.outcome: Both resources remain sellable until prepare requests arrive.
frames.invariant: No participant may commit TX-42 without a durable global decision.

frames.title: Prepare the flight
frames.narration: Flight inventory durably reserves seat 12A and promises not to give it to another transaction.
frames.outcome: Seat 12A is locked even though the trip is not committed.
frames.invariant: A YES vote means the participant can later commit despite a restart.

frames.title: Prepare the hotel
frames.narration: Hotel inventory writes its prepared record and holds room 504.
frames.outcome: Every participant has voted YES, but prepared locks still block competing buyers.
frames.invariant: The coordinator chooses COMMIT only after every required YES vote.

frames.title: Make commit durable
frames.narration: The coordinator appends COMMIT before telling suppliers, so recovery cannot choose a different answer.
frames.outcome: TX-42 is committed logically even before all acknowledgements arrive.
frames.invariant: Once logged, the global decision is immutable and replayable.

frames.title: Finish after a lost message
frames.narration: The flight learns COMMIT immediately; the hotel learns the same decision from recovery replay.
frames.outcome: The traveler owns both reservations; retries cannot split the decision.
frames.invariant: All prepared participants eventually apply the same logged outcome.

mechanism.scenario: A warehouse fleet switches two loading robots to a new route under bounded-delay assumptions.

frames.title: Propose the route
frames.narration: The controller asks whether both robots can safely adopt route R2.
frames.outcome: No robot has crossed the point where it expects a commit.
frames.invariant: A NO reply or expired first-phase deadline causes ABORT.

frames.title: Collect unanimous readiness
frames.narration: Both robots report that route R2 is feasible and reserve their next movement slot.
frames.outcome: The controller may enter the extra pre-commit phase.
frames.invariant: PRE_COMMIT is sent only after unanimous YES replies.

frames.title: Enter pre-commit
frames.narration: Each robot acknowledges PRE_COMMIT, learning that every participant was ready.
frames.outcome: Participants now distinguish unanimous readiness from an uncertain prepare.
frames.invariant: A pre-committed participant must not independently abort.

frames.title: Use the timeout assumption
frames.narration: The controller pauses, but the watchdog confirms the modeled bounded delay rather than a partition.
frames.outcome: Robot Beacon can seek peers and progress only because timing and failure assumptions hold.
frames.invariant: Non-blocking progress is unsafe if a network partition can mimic controller failure.

frames.title: Commit the route change
frames.narration: Recovery establishes that PRE_COMMIT was reached, and both robots activate R2.
frames.outcome: Both robots follow R2; the lesson exposes why real partitions undermine 3PC guarantees.
frames.invariant: Commit safety depends on the stated bounded-delay and no-partition model.

distributed-transactions::Saga pattern.title: Saga pattern
distributed-transactions::Saga pattern.summary: A durable sequence of local transactions uses compensations when a later step fails.
distributed-transactions::Saga pattern.tradeoff: Intermediate states are visible and rollback is semantic.

mechanism.scenario: A concert package reserves a ticket, books a train, then compensates both when the hotel sells out.

frames.title: Open the package saga
frames.narration: PKG-8 starts with a durable pointer to the first local transaction.
frames.outcome: Recovery can resume PKG-8 without a global database transaction.
frames.invariant: Progress is durable before a command may be retried.

frames.title: Reserve the concert ticket
frames.narration: The box office commits its own transaction; the reservation is now externally visible.
frames.outcome: Ticket success does not imply package success.
frames.invariant: Every committed forward step has a defined semantic compensation.

frames.title: Book the train
frames.narration: The rail reservation service commits seat C7 and the saga advances to the hotel.
frames.outcome: Two independent local commits exist at once.
frames.invariant: Forward steps execute in saga order and are idempotent.

frames.title: Detect the sold-out hotel
frames.narration: Room H-3 is sold before the command arrives, so PKG-8 records failure and switches direction.
frames.outcome: The saga cannot roll back databases; it must issue business cancellations.
frames.invariant: A failed later step never erases earlier committed facts.

frames.title: Compensate in reverse order
frames.narration: The train is canceled first and the ticket is then released, with each result recorded.
frames.outcome: PKG-8 ends consistently, although its intermediate reservations were visible.
frames.invariant: Compensations are durable, idempotent, and applied in reverse dependency order.

distributed-transactions::Choreography.title: Choreography
distributed-transactions::Choreography.summary: Services advance a workflow by reacting to one another through events.
distributed-transactions::Choreography.tradeoff: Loose coupling obscures the global state machine.

mechanism.scenario: A farm-box subscription activates through domain events without a central workflow owner.

frames.title: Commit the subscription
frames.narration: The subscription ledger creates SUB-31 and emits a fact after its local commit.
frames.outcome: No coordinator tells downstream owners what to do.
frames.invariant: An event describes a committed fact, not a request for an uncommitted change.

frames.title: Allocate produce reactively
frames.narration: Harvest consumes SubscriptionStarted and commits crate C-88 for SUB-31.
frames.outcome: Harvest advances the workflow using only the event contract.
frames.invariant: Consumers deduplicate by event identity before committing local effects.

frames.title: Schedule delivery
frames.narration: Courier reacts to CrateAllocated and reserves stop D-14.
frames.outcome: The global path emerges from subscriptions rather than one visible state machine.
frames.invariant: Every event handler commits locally before publishing its successor fact.

frames.title: Charge after scheduling
frames.narration: Billing consumes DeliveryScheduled and captures the weekly fee.
frames.outcome: SUB-31 is operational across four autonomous owners.
frames.invariant: Event ordering for SUB-31 is preserved by its stream key.

frames.title: Ignore duplicate delivery
frames.narration: A redelivered DeliveryScheduled event is recognized by its event ID and does not charge twice.
frames.outcome: At-least-once delivery does not create a second $24 charge.
frames.invariant: Each subscriber owns durable idempotency for the events it consumes.

distributed-transactions::Orchestration.title: Orchestration
distributed-transactions::Orchestration.summary: A durable coordinator commands steps and tracks replies, retries, timeouts, and compensation.

mechanism.scenario: A passport renewal coordinator orders photo review, fee capture, printing, and recovery.

frames.title: Persist the workflow
frames.narration: The coordinator stores APP-73 and its first command before dispatch.
frames.outcome: A crash cannot lose which command must run next.
frames.invariant: Workflow state and command identity are durable before delivery.

frames.title: Accept the portrait
frames.narration: Photo review handles a correlated command and returns PhotoAccepted.
frames.outcome: The coordinator makes the global next step explicit.
frames.invariant: Replies advance only the matching application and command.

frames.title: Capture the renewal fee
frames.narration: The fee ledger captures exactly $130 under stable charge ID CH-73.
frames.outcome: Payment success is recorded before printing is commanded.
frames.invariant: Command handlers are idempotent under their stable business IDs.

frames.title: Recover a printing timeout
frames.narration: No reply arrives, so the coordinator reloads PRINT_PENDING and retries B-73.
frames.outcome: Recovery resumes the pending transition instead of restarting the renewal.
frames.invariant: A timeout means outcome unknown, not operation failed.

frames.title: Complete once
frames.narration: The printer returns BookletPrinted; a duplicate reply cannot advance APP-73 again.
frames.outcome: APP-73 finishes with one fee and one booklet.
frames.invariant: Terminal workflow state is durable and duplicate replies are harmless.

distributed-transactions::Compensating t.title: Compensating transactions
distributed-transactions::Compensating t.summary: Business actions counteract previously committed steps and must be idempotent and recoverable.
distributed-transactions::Compensating t.tradeoff: Compensation may not restore the exact prior state.

mechanism.scenario: A bakery cancels a wedding order after flour was allocated and a courier deposit was paid.

frames.title: Commit the ingredient allocation
frames.narration: The pantry removes 20 kg from free stock for WO-55.
frames.outcome: The allocation is a committed business fact, not an open database transaction.
frames.invariant: Compensation must respect current business reality rather than erase history.

frames.title: Pay the courier deposit
frames.narration: A second local transaction transfers the nonzero delivery deposit.
frames.outcome: Two effects must be counteracted if the order is canceled.
frames.invariant: Every reverse action has a stable idempotency key.

frames.title: Record customer cancellation
frames.narration: The customer cancels after 5 kg was already mixed, changing what restoration is possible.
frames.outcome: Exact rollback is impossible because consumed flour cannot be un-mixed.
frames.invariant: The compensating plan is based on present state and domain policy.

frames.title: Refund the deposit idempotently
frames.narration: Refund key REF-DEP-55 returns $60; a retry observes the existing journal row.
frames.outcome: The courier balance is restored without a double refund.
frames.invariant: Repeating REF-DEP-55 produces the same single financial effect.

frames.title: Return what remains
frames.narration: The pantry returns 15 usable kilograms and records 5 kilograms as cancellation waste.
frames.outcome: The order resolves honestly: money restored, reusable stock returned, waste retained.
frames.invariant: Completion records both successful compensation and irrecoverable residual effects.

distributed-transactions::MVCC.title: MVCC
distributed-transactions::MVCC.summary: Multiple versions let readers use stable snapshots while writers create new committed versions.
distributed-transactions::MVCC.tradeoff: Long snapshots increase storage and cleanup pressure.

mechanism.scenario: A library catalog lets a long report read book availability while a checkout creates a newer row version.

frames.title: Pin a read snapshot
frames.narration: The report starts at timestamp 40 and sees BK-10 version 38 as available.
frames.outcome: The report has a stable visibility boundary.
frames.invariant: A reader sees the newest committed version not newer than its snapshot.

frames.title: Create instead of overwrite
frames.narration: Checkout transaction 42 writes a private BK-10 version while v38 remains intact.
frames.outcome: Readers and the writer coexist without in-place overwrite.
frames.invariant: Uncommitted versions are invisible to other transactions.

frames.title: Commit the new version
frames.narration: The checkout commits version 43 with borrower Maya.
frames.outcome: New transactions see v43 while the report still sees v38.
frames.invariant: Commit adds a visibility interval; it does not rewrite an older snapshot.

frames.title: Preserve repeatable reading
frames.narration: The report rereads BK-10 and still receives v38 because timestamp 43 is in its future.
frames.outcome: The long report is internally consistent without blocking checkout.
frames.invariant: Visibility is determined by version timestamps and transaction ownership.

frames.title: Reclaim after snapshot release
frames.narration: When the report ends, no active snapshot needs v38 and vacuum removes it.
frames.outcome: Storage is recovered only after visibility safety permits it.
frames.invariant: Vacuum never removes a version visible to any active snapshot.

entities.description: stores Alice and Ben on-call flags

entities.label: Alice leave transaction
entities.description: reads snapshot S=70 and updates Alice

entities.label: Ben leave transaction
entities.description: reads snapshot S=70 and updates Ben

entities.label: Coverage rule
entities.description: requires at least one surgeon on call

frames.title: Start from valid coverage
frames.narration: Both surgeons are on call when snapshot 70 is established.
frames.outcome: The coverage invariant initially holds.
frames.invariant: Each transaction reads one stable committed snapshot.

frames.title: Alice approves leave
frames.narration: Alice sees Ben on call and prepares to set only her own row to OFF.
frames.outcome: Alice reasons correctly within snapshot 70.
frames.invariant: Reads do not change when concurrent transactions later commit.

frames.title: Ben approves leave
frames.narration: Ben sees Alice on call in the same snapshot and writes a different row.
frames.outcome: The transactions do not have a direct write-write conflict.
frames.invariant: Snapshot isolation commonly rejects concurrent writes to the same item, not disjoint items.

frames.title: Commit both disjoint writes
frames.narration: Alice commits at 71 and Ben commits at 72 because their write sets do not overlap.
frames.outcome: Write skew violates coverage despite repeatable reads and no dirty data.
frames.invariant: Snapshot isolation alone does not guarantee arbitrary cross-row invariants.

frames.title: Make the conflict explicit
frames.narration: A repair transaction restores Ben and future leave requests lock a shared coverage row.
frames.outcome: Materializing the invariant creates a write conflict that snapshot isolation can detect.
frames.invariant: Critical predicates require explicit locking, constraint design, or serializable isolation.

distributed-transactions::Serializable t.title: Serializable transactions
distributed-transactions::Serializable t.summary: Concurrent transactions produce an outcome equivalent to some serial execution.

mechanism.scenario: Two bidders concurrently try to buy the final numbered charity print for different prices.

frames.title: Begin concurrent purchases
frames.narration: Nora and Omar start while print #1 is unsold.
frames.outcome: Concurrency is allowed until conflicts require ordering.
frames.invariant: Committed behavior must equal some one-at-a-time execution.

frames.title: Track Nora read
frames.narration: Nora reads owner=NULL and the engine records the read dependency.
frames.outcome: The read is evidence used during commit validation.
frames.invariant: Relevant reads and writes participate in concurrency control.

frames.title: Commit Omar first
frames.narration: Omar writes ownership and commits version 11 before Nora validates.
frames.outcome: Omar establishes the candidate serial order.
frames.invariant: Only one committed transaction may consume the final print.

frames.title: Abort the incompatible commit
frames.narration: Nora validation detects that her decision depended on the pre-Omar version and aborts.
frames.outcome: The engine sacrifices one transaction rather than commit a nonserializable history.
frames.invariant: Serialization failures are expected control flow and must be retried as whole transactions.

frames.title: Retry against the winner
frames.narration: Nora retries, now reads owner=OMAR, and records a clean sold-out result.
frames.outcome: The final state matches Omar followed by Nora.
frames.invariant: Retries re-execute all reads under a fresh serializable transaction.

frames.narration: Window 200 ends with eight admitted requests recorded for interpolation.

frames.invariant: Rotation must atomically preserve the completed count and clear the new current bucket.

frames.title: History begins decaying
frames.narration: At four seconds into window 201, the prior count has weight 56/60.
frames.outcome: The recent burst still fills the estimated trailing window.
frames.invariant: The historical contribution decreases continuously rather than resetting at a boundary.

frames.title: Decay permits an admission
frames.narration: At sixteen seconds, weighted history is 5.87, so the projected count 6.87 admits one request.
frames.outcome: Time decay opens capacity gradually.
frames.invariant: The estimator uses the count before the candidate request, then increments only on admission.

frames.title: Current traffic fills estimate
frames.narration: At thirty seconds, two more requests project counts six and seven, raising the current counter to three.
frames.outcome: The combined weighted history and active count reaches the limit.
frames.invariant: Both counters for one key must be read and updated under a consistent rotation epoch.

frames.title: At-limit request rejected
frames.narration: A request one tenth of a second later projects 7.99 and leaves the current count unchanged.
frames.outcome: The candidate would push the estimate above seven.
frames.invariant: Admission compares the projected count, not merely the stored current counter.

frames.title: Further decay reopens capacity
frames.narration: At thirty-eight seconds, the projected count falls to 6.93 and one more request is admitted.
frames.outcome: Admission capacity changes smoothly as historical traffic ages out.
frames.invariant: The two-counter approximation bounds storage but is not an exact timestamp log.

storage-systems::Write-ahead logs.title: Write-ahead logs
storage-systems::Write-ahead logs.summary: A write-ahead log durably records mutations before mutable state is acknowledged.
storage-systems::Write-ahead logs.tradeoff: Log sync adds latency and replay time grows without checkpoints.

mechanism.scenario: A database recovers committed balances after a process crash.

frames.title: Begin transaction
frames.narration: Transaction T8 receives LSN 40 before changing pages.
frames.outcome: Recovery can identify T8.
frames.invariant: Log sequence numbers strictly increase.

frames.title: Log updates
frames.narration: Redo/undo records capture A:100→90 and B:50→60 before dirtying memory pages.
frames.outcome: Memory reflects the transfer.
frames.invariant: The update log record exists before its page may flush.

frames.title: Force commit record
frames.narration: LSNs 41 through 43, including COMMIT, are flushed atomically to stable storage.
frames.outcome: The client may receive success.
frames.invariant: Commit is acknowledged only after its log record is durable.

frames.title: Crash before page flush
frames.narration: The process loses dirty memory pages; disk still contains old balances.
frames.outcome: Committed data pages lag the durable log.
frames.invariant: Stable WAL survives process failure.

frames.title: Redo committed updates
frames.narration: Recovery replays LSNs 41 and 42 because page LSNs are older.
frames.outcome: Committed balances are restored.
frames.invariant: Redo is idempotent when guarded by page LSN.

storage-systems::Memtables.title: Memtables
storage-systems::Memtables.summary: Memtables hold recent sorted writes in memory before immutable flush.
storage-systems::Memtables.tradeoff: Memory is bounded, and unflushed data relies on the write-ahead log.

mechanism.scenario: An LSM engine orders recent writes in a skip-list memtable.

frames.title: Ordered writes
frames.narration: The mutable skip list contains a, c, and d in key order.
frames.outcome: Recent values are searchable in memory.
frames.invariant: Level zero contains every key in sorted order.

frames.title: Search towers
frames.narration: Lookup c advances on level 2 to a, drops, then advances to c.
frames.outcome: c is found without scanning every key.
frames.invariant: Traversal never moves past the target key.

frames.title: Overwrite in place
frames.narration: A newer write c→8 replaces the visible value for c.
frames.outcome: Reads now return 8.
frames.invariant: At most one current entry per key is visible in this memtable.

frames.title: Reach size threshold
frames.narration: Adding e and f pushes estimated memory beyond 100 bytes.
frames.outcome: The active memtable must rotate.
frames.invariant: Writes remain ordered while mutable.

frames.title: Freeze and rotate
frames.narration: The full table becomes immutable and a new empty mutable table accepts writes.
frames.outcome: The immutable table is ready to flush.
frames.invariant: Frozen entries never mutate; new writes use a fresh table.

storage-systems::Compaction.title: Compaction
storage-systems::Compaction.summary: Compaction merges sorted files, removes obsolete versions, and restores storage-level invariants.
storage-systems::Compaction.tradeoff: Consumes I/O and CPU and can create latency spikes.

mechanism.scenario: An LSM store merges versions and tombstones to control read amplification.

frames.title: Choose overlap
frames.narration: Runs R3, R2, and R1 overlap key range a..f.
frames.outcome: All versions in the overlap enter one merge.
frames.invariant: Inputs are individually sorted.

frames.title: Merge smallest keys
frames.narration: The heap emits a from R2, then sees two versions of b.
frames.outcome: Newest b→9 replaces b→2.
frames.invariant: Only the newest visible version of a key is emitted.

frames.title: Continue ordered merge
frames.narration: c is emitted; d's tombstone supersedes older d→4.
frames.outcome: The delete marker remains authoritative.
frames.invariant: A tombstone participates as the newest version.

frames.title: Drop safe tombstone
frames.narration: Because this is the bottom level, no older d can exist below; the tombstone is discarded.
frames.outcome: Deleted key d consumes no output space.
frames.invariant: A tombstone is dropped only when no older version can reappear.

frames.title: Install output
frames.narration: f completes the sorted run and input files become obsolete.
frames.outcome: Three overlapping runs become one compact run.
frames.invariant: Output is sorted, nonduplicated, and preserves newest visibility.

storage-systems::Bloom filters.title: Bloom filters
storage-systems::Bloom filters.summary: A Bloom filter probabilistically proves many keys are absent without reading storage.
storage-systems::Bloom filters.tradeoff: False positives remain and filters consume memory; false negatives are forbidden.

mechanism.scenario: An SSTable reader uses a three-hash Bloom filter to avoid disk probes while tracking false-positive pressure.

frames.title: Seed the filter
frames.narration: Inserted keys set positions 1, 3, 5, 7, and 10 in the twelve-bit array.
frames.outcome: The filter summarizes keys already written to the SSTable.
frames.invariant: Insertion only sets bits; it never clears them.

frames.title: Hash a definite miss
frames.narration: Key kiwi maps to positions 1, 4, and 10.
frames.outcome: The reader has three concrete positions to test.
frames.invariant: A query uses the same hash functions as insertion.

frames.title: Reject on a zero
frames.narration: Position 4 is zero, proving kiwi is absent without reading the SSTable.
frames.outcome: One disk probe is avoided.
frames.invariant: Any queried zero forbids a false negative.

frames.title: Verify a possible match
frames.narration: Key lime maps to 1, 5, and 10; all are one, so the SSTable must verify it.
frames.outcome: The positive filter answer becomes an exact disk lookup.
frames.invariant: Bloom positives are candidates, never proof.

frames.title: Expose false-positive pressure
frames.narration: After more inserts set nine of twelve bits, pear finds three ones but is absent on disk.
frames.outcome: High occupancy causes an unnecessary read and signals filter rotation or resizing.
frames.invariant: False-positive probability rises as the bit array fills.

storage-systems::Indexing.title: Indexing
storage-systems::Indexing.summary: Indexing builds auxiliary structures that map query keys to records or storage locations.
storage-systems::Indexing.tradeoff: Improves reads while adding storage, write amplification, and freshness lag.

mechanism.scenario: A primary-key index maps account IDs to exact heap-row locations and verifies the base row after lookup.

frames.title: Separate index and heap
frames.narration: The index stores ordered key-to-location entries while heap page p7 stores the complete account row.
frames.outcome: Keys are smaller than full rows and can be searched independently.
frames.invariant: Each live index pointer resolves to one base-row slot.

frames.title: Descend by key
frames.narration: ID 42 falls between root separators 20 and 50.
frames.outcome: The middle leaf is selected.
frames.invariant: Traversal follows the only child range that can contain the key.

frames.title: Resolve the pointer
frames.narration: The leaf entry 42→p7:1 supplies the physical heap location.
frames.outcome: The engine avoids scanning unrelated heap pages.
frames.invariant: Index order determines location, not row truth.

frames.title: Fetch and verify
frames.narration: Heap page p7 slot 1 is read and its row ID is checked against 42.
frames.outcome: The complete Ada row is returned.
frames.invariant: A lookup verifies the base-row key before returning data.

frames.title: Maintain on movement
frames.narration: Vacuum moves row 42 to p9:0 and atomically updates its leaf pointer.
frames.outcome: Future lookups follow the new location.
frames.invariant: An index entry and its referenced row must not remain durably inconsistent.

storage-systems::Secondary indexes.title: Secondary indexes
storage-systems::Secondary indexes.summary: Secondary indexes support lookup by non-primary attributes.
storage-systems::Secondary indexes.tradeoff: Distributed maintenance and uniqueness require coordination or eventual repair.

mechanism.scenario: An email secondary index finds customer rows by a non-primary attribute and verifies stale entries against base data.

frames.title: Index duplicate values
frames.narration: The non-unique email entry stores primary keys 17 and 42 rather than complete rows.
frames.outcome: One secondary key can fan out to multiple base records.
frames.invariant: Posting primary keys keeps the secondary structure compact.

frames.title: Seek the email
frames.narration: The B-tree seek for ada@example returns candidate primary keys 17 and 42.
frames.outcome: Two exact base-row reads are planned.
frames.invariant: Candidates come only from the matching secondary entry.

frames.title: Verify base rows
frames.narration: Rows 17 and 42 still contain ada@example, so both satisfy the predicate.
frames.outcome: Both customer rows are returned.
frames.invariant: Base-row verification protects reads during asynchronous maintenance.

frames.title: Change one attribute
frames.narration: Customer 42 changes to dee@example before the old secondary entry is removed.
frames.outcome: Verification suppresses stale candidate 42.
frames.invariant: A stale index may add false candidates but must not create false query results.

frames.title: Apply index maintenance
frames.narration: The updater removes 42 from ada@example and adds it under dee@example.
frames.outcome: The secondary index converges with base rows.
frames.invariant: Every committed attribute eventually has exactly one corresponding posting per row.

storage-systems::Inverted indexes.title: Inverted indexes
storage-systems::Inverted indexes.summary: Inverted indexes map terms or features to postings lists of matching documents.
storage-systems::Inverted indexes.tradeoff: Text analysis and updates add substantial storage and write cost.

mechanism.scenario: A document store builds term postings with document IDs, frequencies, and positions, then intersects them for an AND query.

frames.title: Publish postings
frames.narration: The lexicon points to sorted postings that carry term frequency and token positions.
frames.outcome: Each term can be retrieved without scanning documents.
frames.invariant: Every posting list is strictly ordered by document ID.

frames.title: Resolve both terms
frames.narration: The dictionary maps distributed to offset 120 and storage to offset 188.
frames.outcome: Two posting streams are opened.
frames.invariant: Dictionary document frequency matches each posting-list length.

frames.title: Advance smaller doc IDs
frames.narration: d1 is below d2, then d2 is below d4, so cursors advance without base reads.
frames.outcome: Both cursors arrive at d4.
frames.invariant: Advancing the smaller ID cannot skip an intersection.

frames.title: Intersect equal postings
frames.narration: Equal IDs d4 and d7 enter the candidate result.
frames.outcome: The AND query has two candidates.
frames.invariant: A document matches only if it appears in every required posting list.

frames.title: Verify document constraints
frames.narration: Base documents confirm d4 and d7 are live and satisfy any non-indexed filters.
frames.outcome: The store returns two exact documents with ranking features.
frames.invariant: Posting candidates are checked against document liveness and residual predicates.

storage-systems::Sparse indexes.title: Sparse indexes
storage-systems::Sparse indexes.summary: Sparse indexes store entries for selected block boundaries rather than every row.
storage-systems::Sparse indexes.tradeoff: Compact and cache-friendly but require scanning within the located block.

mechanism.scenario: A sorted file uses one index entry per data block, then scans inside the selected block for an exact key.

frames.title: Index block boundaries
frames.narration: Only first keys 1, 21, and 41 are stored for three sorted blocks.
frames.outcome: Three entries cover sixty records.
frames.invariant: Each entry names the first key of one non-overlapping sorted block.

frames.title: Floor-search the index
frames.narration: For key 37, the greatest boundary not exceeding it is 21.
frames.outcome: The lookup selects B1.
frames.invariant: The predecessor boundary identifies the only possible block.

frames.title: Scan within B1
frames.narration: The reader checks keys 21 through 37 inside the block.
frames.outcome: Key 37 is found after a bounded local scan.
frames.invariant: Sparse indexing trades index size for within-block work.

frames.title: Stop an absent lookup
frames.narration: For key 39, B1 reaches key 40 without equality and stops before B2.
frames.outcome: No other block can contain 39.
frames.invariant: Sorted, disjoint ranges make the absence conclusion exact.

frames.title: Handle a new block
frames.narration: Appending B3 for keys 61..80 adds only boundary entry 61→B3.
frames.outcome: Index growth follows block count, not row count.
frames.invariant: Every published block has one ordered boundary entry.

storage-systems::Covering indexes.title: Covering indexes
storage-systems::Covering indexes.summary: A covering index contains every field needed by a query, avoiding base-record reads.
storage-systems::Covering indexes.tradeoff: Larger indexes increase write and storage costs.

mechanism.scenario: A covering index answers an active-user projection from indexed columns and visits the base table only for an uncovered field.

frames.title: Store included columns
frames.narration: The index key status includes projected columns id and name in each leaf entry.
frames.outcome: The leaf can satisfy status, id, and name without heap data.
frames.invariant: A query is covered only when every required column exists in the index.

frames.title: Seek active entries
frames.narration: The engine reads the contiguous active range from the leaf.
frames.outcome: Two qualifying entries are available.
frames.invariant: Index key order groups equal status values.

frames.title: Return index-only rows
frames.narration: Included values directly produce (17,Ada) and (42,Bo).
frames.outcome: The query completes with zero base-page reads.
frames.invariant: Index-only output must come from a visibility-valid entry.

frames.title: Request an uncovered field
frames.narration: Adding city to the projection makes the index non-covering.
frames.outcome: Primary-key pointers schedule two heap fetches.
frames.invariant: Missing projected columns require base-row access.

frames.title: Join base values
frames.narration: Rows 17 and 42 supply SEA and DAL and are rechecked as active.
frames.outcome: The expanded projection is exact but costs two reads.
frames.invariant: Base verification remains authoritative for uncovered data.
